name: Kaiming Liu
title: Physics PhD student
description: Kaiming Liu is a Physics PhD student at UIUC studying scientific machine learning, inverse problems, and simulation-to-experiment robustness.
bio: I work on scientific machine learning and inverse problems: inferring physical models from measurements and understanding uncertainty in those models.

Previously, I studied thin-film materials with molecular beam epitaxy and scanning tunneling microscopy in Vidya Madhavan’s group. That experimental background motivates my interest in connecting simulations to real measurements.

research.title: Probabilistic inference for physical models
research.text: My current work explores probabilistic, multimodal inference for crystal electric field inverse problems. I use physics-based forward reconstruction to assess parameters that can explain the same measurements.

research.title: From simulation to experiment
research.text: I study how experimental noise and distribution shift affect inference trained on simulations, particularly in magnetic and scattering inverse problems.

research.title: Computational many-body physics
research.text: I also work on neural-network backflow wavefunctions and variational Monte Carlo for strongly correlated fermions, including numerical implementation and parallel sampling.

background: In Vidya Madhavan’s group at UIUC, I grew thin-film heterostructures with MBE, used STM/STS in ultrahigh vacuum, and developed temperature-control and data-analysis tools. Earlier research included Rydberg-atom simulations at Xi’an Jiaotong University and STM research in Michael F. Crommie’s group at UC Berkeley.
interests: Scientific machine learning; inverse problems; probabilistic inference; simulation-to-experiment transfer; computational condensed matter physics.

education.degree: Special Class for the Gifted Young

experience.role: Graduate research, Bryan K. Clark group
bullets: Develop probabilistic and multimodal inference for crystal electric field inverse problems, with physics-based forward reconstruction of observables.
Study robustness to experimental noise and simulation-to-experiment distribution shift in magnetic and scattering inverse problems.
Implemented neural-network backflow wavefunctions and variational Monte Carlo for correlated fermions, with parallel cluster sampling and reuse of wavefunction evaluations.
Grew thin-film heterostructures by molecular beam epitaxy and characterized materials with STM/STS in ultrahigh vacuum.
Automated MBE temperature control with feedback, measurement logging, and alerts for repeatable growth protocols.
Developed Python and MATLAB STM/STS analysis, including constant-energy contours and joint-density-of-states calculations for quasiparticle interference.
Simulated Rydberg-atom dynamics and photon-mediated interactions with MATLAB and Python to study quantum nonlinear optics.
Built a discrete-time lattice simulation to examine two-qubit phase-flip dynamics and explore many-body regimes.

experience.role: Research assistant, Michael F. Crommie group
bullets: Assisted with synthesis and STM characterization of graphene nanoribbons containing five-membered rings, supporting studies of their electronic states.

teaching.text: Led discussion and laboratory sections, held office hours, and provided feedback on assignments in electromagnetism and modern physics.
